newsitem.title: USA: Clinton Medicare plan gets tough Senate reception.
newsitem.headline: Clinton Medicare plan gets tough Senate reception.

text.p: President Clinton's recently unveiled Medicare plan was billed as an effort to meet Republicans halfway on the sensitive issue, but lawmakers made it clear Thursday the White House still has miles to go.

Republicans, and some Democrats, warned the White House at a Senate Budget Committee hearing that they had serious concerns with the plan Clinton announced earlier this week to reduce Medicare spending by $138 billion over six years.

Lawmakers from both parties cautioned that the White House proposal to cut spending on health maintenance organizations by $46 billion over six years went too far and could make it tough to expand managed care to the 38 million senior citizens who rely on Medicare.
"This will discriminate against the good guys and ... I will oppose it strongly," said Oregon Democratic Sen. Ron Wyden.

Republicans were scathing in their criticism of a Clinton proposal to transfer part of Medicare's fast-growing home health program from the Part A hospital trust fund, which faces impending bankruptcy, to another Medicare trust fund.

Republicans estimated the White House plan would move upwards of $100 billion in ten-year home health costs out of Part A, which is funded by payroll taxes. They called it a "gimmick" and "shell game" that made the Part A trust fund, now expected to go bankrupt in 2001, appear more robust.
Texas Republican Sen. Phil Gramm termed the transfer "completely beyond the range of possibility" predicting there was "not a chance in the world" it would pass a key panel.
Office of Management and Budget deputy director Jacob Lew, testifying before the committee, did not provide figures for the size of the transfer but said it was under $100 billion.

Lew said that by using the home health transfer, the White House was able to ensure the solvency of the Medicare Part A trust fund through the start of 2007 -- fulfilling a promise to protect the program for a decade.
"This policy avoids the need for excessive reductions in payments to hospitals, physicians and other health care providers while helping to extend the solvency of the Part A trust fund," Lew said.
He also defended the White House plan to cut payments to HMOS, saying data showed Medicare was paying them too much and losing money on every senior citizen who chose managed care.
Other witnesses said HMO cost controls were possible, but the White House plan for across-the-board cuts was not the right way.

Clearly were still licking their wounds from the November elections when Democrats attacked them for a failed proposal to reduce Medicare by $270 billion, Republicans complained the Clinton plan addressed only short term concerns and did not deal with the long term financial programs that threaten the program as baby boomers retire.

Not all reviews were negative. The White House plan does include deeper reductions that Clinton proposed last year. The overall plan carefully avoids big increases in premiums for senior citizens, getting most of its savings from hospitals, doctors and other health providers. It would expand benefits under Medicare by about $22 billion over six years.
